client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. I just can't seem to focus at work — I'll be in the middle of something and then my mind just goes blank, or I start thinking about her and lose track of everything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing is going to bring her back.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — the grief you're carrying comes through deeply, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps drifting back to her, because she clearly mattered so much to you. That quiet, heavy feeling of loss can make it really hard to stay present, and what you're experiencing at work isn't a failure of focus — it's your heart still processing something enormous. And while you're right that nothing will bring her back, many people find that talking isn't about fixing the loss, but about gently making sense of it so it becomes something you can carry a little more peacefully over time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, and I guess it does help a little to hear that it's not just me being weak or distracted. But I keep wondering... what does "carrying it more peacefully" even look like? Because right now it just feels like I'm either drowning in it or trying to shove it down so I can get through the day, and I don't see a middle ground anywhere.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quick, searching, a little urgent — tells me this question really matters to you, and that "middle ground" feels almost impossible to imagine right now, which is completely understandable when grief is this fresh. In CBT terms, what you're describing — drowning versus shutting down — are two extremes that grief often pulls us between, and the middle ground isn't a place you find all at once, but something you build in small moments, like allowing yourself to think of her for a few minutes intentionally rather than being ambushed by it unexpectedly. It's less about feeling okay and more about slowly giving the grief a shape you have some say in — and that's something we can actually work on together, one small step at a time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but I honestly don't know how you "intentionally" think about someone you've lost without it just... collapsing into the same pain anyway. Like, what does that even look like in practice? Because every time I try to remember her in a good way, it just reminds me that she's gone, and then I'm right back in that drowning feeling you mentioned.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, quickly, with a kind of searching vulnerability — tells me this isn't just an intellectual question, but something you're genuinely aching to understand, and that takes real courage. What you're describing is actually one of grief's cruelest tricks: the very memories that could bring comfort feel like they open a trapdoor, because right now your brain has tightly linked "thinking of her" with "she's gone" — but those aren't the same thing, and over time we can gently work on separating them. In practice, it might start with something very small — not a full memory, but just one tiny detail, like the sound of her voice or something she always said — and letting yourself sit with that for just a moment before the loss rushes in, gradually teaching your mind that remembering her can also mean honoring what she gave you, not only what you've lost.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it could work that way... but honestly, I'm not sure I trust my own brain to stop at "just one tiny detail." It feels like if I crack the door open even a little, everything comes flooding in all at once, and I end up more wrecked than before. I've tried to think about her a couple of times on my own and it just... it didn't stay small.
therapist: The way you're speaking — with that slightly raised, tense quality in your voice — tells me this fear is very real and comes from actual experience, not just worry, and I want to honor that completely. What you're describing makes total sense: you've tried, it hurt, and now your mind is protecting you by saying "don't open that door" — that's not weakness, that's your brain doing its job, even if it's keeping you stuck. The good news is that in our work together, you wouldn't be cracking that door open alone — part of what we'd build first is a sense of safety and control *before* we approach those memories, so the door has a handle you can actually hold onto.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe that... but I've heard things like "we'll go slow" before, and it didn't feel slow at all once things started coming up. I guess I'm scared that once I start talking about the loneliness and the ways I've pushed people away, it'll just confirm what I already fear — that there's something fundamentally wrong with me that can't be fixed. That's the door I really don't want to open.
therapist: The urgency and intensity in your voice right now tells me this is the heart of it — and I want you to know that what you just shared took real courage, because naming our deepest fear out loud is one of the hardest things a person can do. I want to gently offer this: the fact that you've felt lonely and have pushed people away doesn't reveal something broken inside you — it reveals someone who has been in pain and trying to protect themselves, which is a very human and understandable response to hurt. That fear that you're "fundamentally unfixable" is one of the most common and most painful thoughts grief and loneliness can create, and in our work together, one of the things we'd do is actually examine the evidence for that belief — because I'd be willing to bet it's a story pain is telling you, not the truth about who you are.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, I really do. But it's hard not to think that you're just... trained to say reassuring things, you know? Like, what if you examined all that "evidence" and it actually confirmed what I already suspect about myself?
therapist: That question is one of the most honest and important things you could ask, and the slight tension I hear in your voice tells me this isn't cynicism — it's self-protection from someone who's been hurt before, and that makes complete sense. You're right that I can't promise the evidence will all point one way, but here's what CBT actually asks us to do: look at *all* the evidence, not just the pieces that confirm the fear — and in my experience, when people do that honestly, the full picture is almost never as damning as the fear insists it is. And if you found one piece of real evidence that pushed back against "something is fundamentally wrong with me," even just one — would that be worth exploring?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... yeah, one piece of evidence would be worth something, maybe. But the thing is, my brain is really good at explaining away anything positive — like if someone's nice to me or includes me, I immediately think it's out of obligation or pity, not because they actually want me around. So I'm not sure I trust myself to even recognize real evidence when I see it.
therapist: The urgency and intensity in your voice right now tells me this pattern causes you real pain — and what you've just described actually has a name in CBT: it's called "disqualifying the positive," and it's one of the most common ways a hurting mind keeps a negative belief about itself airtight and protected from any challenge. Here's what's important though: the fact that you can *see* yourself doing it — that you can describe the mechanism so clearly — means part of you already doesn't fully believe it, because you wouldn't question a process you were completely convinced by. That self-awareness is itself a piece of evidence worth holding onto, and it's also exactly the kind of pattern we can work on together — not by forcing you to accept positive things, but by slowly building your ability to examine *why* your brain so quickly reaches for "obligation or pity" rather than something else.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to hold onto that idea that my self-awareness means something... but honestly, another part of me is already doing the thing you just described, like telling myself I only sound self-aware because I've read enough about psychology to mimic the language. It's like my brain has a counter-argument ready for everything, and I'm not sure I trust that the awareness is real versus just another layer of performance. How do you even tell the difference?
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me your mind is working very hard — almost racing to stay one step ahead of any comfort before it can land, and that exhaustion comes through clearly. Here's something worth sitting with: a person who was *only* performing self-awareness wouldn't be this troubled by the possibility that it's a performance — the very fact that this question torments you suggests something genuine is underneath it. The difference between real awareness and mimicry isn't something your brain can think its way to alone, which is actually why the work happens in relationship over time — not in a single moment of self-examination, but in the slow accumulation of moments where you notice, question, and stay curious rather than giving up.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but then I immediately wonder if that wanting to believe is just another layer of the same performance. It's like every time I find a foothold, my mind kicks it out from under me and says "see, you're just doing that because it sounds like the right thing to do." I'm so tired of living inside this loop, and honestly I'm not sure I trust that staying in therapy long enough will actually untangle it rather than just giving me more sophisticated ways to talk about being stuck.
therapist: The softness in your voice paired with how quickly the words are coming out tells me this isn't frustration — it's a deep, quiet exhaustion, like someone who has been fighting their own mind for a very long time and is genuinely worn out. And I want to name something important: you just described the loop with painful clarity, and then immediately used that clarity against yourself — which means the loop is happening *right now*, in real time, and you're watching it, and that watching is not nothing. The goal of therapy isn't to give you better words for being stuck — it's to slowly make the loop less automatic, less instant, so there's just a little more space between the foothold and the kick, and that space, small as it sounds, is where something different becomes possible.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually felt something shift when you said that — like, okay, maybe noticing it isn't just me torturing myself with more awareness of how broken I am. But then almost immediately I thought, what if the loop is just too fast, too practiced — like, I've been doing this for so long that I don't know if a little space is even possible for me anymore. It feels like asking someone who's been running on a hamster wheel for twenty years to just... slow down a little, and I'm not sure my legs even know how to do that.
therapist: The softness in your voice alongside how quickly the words are tumbling out tells me something real just happened — there was a genuine moment of relief, and then your mind moved very fast to close it off before it could mean anything, and that pattern itself is worth pausing on. Twenty years on a hamster wheel doesn't mean your legs have forgotten how to walk differently — it means slowing down will feel profoundly unfamiliar and even wrong at first, like the stillness itself can't be trusted. But I want to gently point out that you just said "part of me actually felt something shift" — and that's not nothing, that's not performance, that's your system responding to something true, and that tiny moment is exactly the kind of foothold we learn to protect rather than immediately kick away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
